content: 1. Castor et al. conducted a geospatial and risk-based analysis to estimate the need and impact of HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) in Malawi, Mozambique, and Zambia. Their findings were published in PLoS Medicine in 2021. 2. Ayton SG, Pavlicova M, and Abdool Karim Q developed a novel risk scoring tool to identify adolescent girls and young women for targeted HIV prevention in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. This study was published in Scientific Reports in 2020. 3. Smith DK, Pals SL, Herbst JH, Shinde S, and Carey JW created a clinical screening index to predict new HIV infections among men who have sex with men in the United States. Their work was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2012. 4. Baeten JM, Heffron R, Kidoguchi L, Mugo NR, Katabira E, Bukusi EA, and colleagues conducted a prospective implementation study on the integrated delivery of antiretroviral treatment and PrEP to HIV-1 serodiscordant couples in Kenya and Uganda. This study was published in PLoS Medicine in 2016. 5. Irungu EM, Heffron R, Mugo N, Ngure K, Katabira E, Bulya N, and colleagues utilized a risk scoring tool to identify higher-risk HIV-1 serodiscordant couples for antiretroviral-based HIV-1 prevention interventions. Their findings were published in BMC Infectious Diseases in 2016. 6. Kahle EM, Hughes JP, Lingappa JR, John-Stewart G, Celum C, Nakku-Joloba E, and colleagues developed an empiric risk scoring tool to identify high-risk heterosexual HIV-1 serodiscordant couples for targeted HIV-1 prevention. This study was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2013. 7. Balkus JE, Brown E, Palanee T, Nair G, Gafoor Z, Zhang J, and colleagues created an empiric HIV risk scoring tool to predict HIV-1 acquisition in African women. Their work was published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2016. 8. Pintye J, Drake AL, Kinuthia J, Unger JA, Matemo D, Heffron RA, and colleagues developed a risk assessment tool to identify pregnant and postpartum women who may benefit from PrEP. This study was published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2017. 9. Peebles K, Palanee-Phillips T, Balkus JE, Beesham I, Makkan H, Deese J, and colleagues found that age-specific risk scores do not improve HIV-1 prediction among women in South Africa. Their findings were published in the Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes in 2020. 10. Ayala G, Sprague L, van der Merwe LL-A, Thomas RM, Chang J, Arreola S, and colleagues conducted a scoping review on peerand community-led responses to HIV. This review was published in PLoS One in 2021. 11. The World Health Organization (WHO) published guidelines for the psychosocially assisted pharmacological treatment of opioid dependence, emphasizing the importance of transitioning to digital health systems to improve care delivery and monitoring. 12. WHO recommends promoting the analysis and use of routinely collected HIV testing data to optimize testing services, reach populations with undiagnosed HIV, and support early diagnosis. This includes improving the monitoring of time to diagnosis to facilitate rapid antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation and engagement in care. 13. Person-centered patient data should be used to continuously assess interruptions in HIV treatment, improve re-engagement, and enhance retention in care. This involves strengthening data analysis, tracing interventions, and longitudinal monitoring of ART patients through integrated service delivery. 14. WHO emphasizes the integration and strengthening of data collection and reporting for differentiated service delivery (DSD) within HIV patient monitoring systems. This approach aims to improve treatment outcomes and programmatic efficiency by linking community-delivered services with health facility monitoring. 15. Routine data quality assessments should be incorporated into long-term improvement processes to enhance data use and improve HIV treatment outcomes. This includes integrating assessments of data quality for viral load testing and supporting enhanced data analysis and feedback mechanisms. 16. Aggregated and de-duplicated individual-level patient treatment data should be used to inform drug inventory management, reduce wastage, and prevent stock-outs at national, district, and facility levels. This includes ART, PrEP, and drugs for opportunistic infections and opioid agonist therapy. 17. Investments in digital health information systems (HIS), such as electronic medical records (EMRs) and unique identifiers (UIDs), have strengthened person-centered patient monitoring and service delivery. These systems enable robust longitudinal monitoring and efficient resource allocation. 18. HIV patient monitoring systems should be integrated with monitoring systems for other communicable diseases, such as tuberculosis (TB), viral hepatitis, and sexually transmitted infections (STIs), as well as chronic non-communicable conditions like cardiovascular diseases and diabetes. 19. WHO updated its HIV patient monitoring guidelines to include 80 priority indicators, expanding from the 40 indicators recommended in 2020. These indicators address prevention, ART, DSD, vertical transmission, and TB-HIV co-infection, among other areas. 20. Community-based HIV testing services are recommended for key populations and high-burden settings. Monitoring approaches should be adapted to track service delivery outside health facilities and ensure linkage to care. 21. Retesting all pregnant women with unknown or HIV-negative status in late pregnancy is now recommended in high-burden settings. Monitoring systems must be adapted to support this recommendation. 22. Rapid ART initiation should be offered to all individuals with confirmed HIV diagnosis and clinical assessment, preferably on the same day. Monitoring tools must be updated to track rapid ART initiation. 23. Updated ART regimens and codes reflect new recommendations for preferred firstand second-line antiretroviral regimens, including dolutegravir (DTG)-based regimens for children, adolescents, pregnant women, and adults. 24. The definition of loss to follow-up (LTFU) has been revised from 90 days to 28 days since the last missed appointment. Patient monitoring tools must be updated to reflect this change and support tracing interventions. 25. WHO emphasizes the importance of monitoring retention and total attrition from ART, focusing on measuring programmatic outcomes and improving service delivery efficiency.
